items.text: Decide, act, observe, repeat, inside a loop with a limit
No tool requests: the model has answered
Results go back as user messages, matched by id

captions.text: You know the four parts of an agent.
Now we connect them.
In this lesson we write the agent loop itself: about twenty lines of Python.
We'll go slowly, one small piece at a time, and then run it and look at exactly what
happened.
You'll write a loop that decides, acts, observes, and stops.
You'll send tool results back in the format the API expects.
And you'll follow how the message list grows, turn by turn.
We start with a client, the tool definitions from our project, and the message list.
Right now the list holds just one message: the user's question, which needs two
calculations.
Then the loop.
Notice it's a for loop that runs at most five times, not a while true loop.
If something goes wrong, this agent can never run forever.
Always give a loop a limit.
Step one, decide.
We send the tools and the whole message list to the model, and it decides what to do
next.
We add the model's reply to the list, exactly as it came back.
Don't edit it, and don't rebuild it.
The next request must contain it unchanged.
Now we look for tool requests in the reply.
If there aren't any, the model has finished, so we print its answer and stop.
That's step four, stop.
Otherwise, step two, act.
For each tool request, our code runs the tool, using the name and the input the
model gave us.
Step three, observe.
We wrap each output in a tool result.
The tool use ID connects the result to the request it answers.
That's why every request has an ID.
And we add the results to the list as a user message.
Then the loop goes round again, and the model decides with the new information.
Let's run it.
Again, the offline fake plays the model, following a fixed script, but the loop is
exactly the code you just read.
Turn one: the model asks for eighteen times one point one five, and our code returns
twenty point seven.
Turn two: it asks for twenty point seven divided by three, and gets six point nine.
Turn three: no more tool requests, so it answers, and the loop stops.
Offline, that answer is a placeholder that lists the results.
The script printed six messages.
Let's walk through them, because this list is the agent's memory.
One: the user's question.
Two: the model's first tool request.
Three: our result, sent as a user message.
Four: the second tool request.
Five: the second result.
And six: the final answer.
Three requests in total, and each one sent the whole list so far.
When you build a loop like this, three rules matter.
First, tool results always go back in a user message.
Second, every tool request needs a result with the same ID.
If the model asks for two tools at once, send back two results.
And third, send the model's replies back unchanged.
Current models check that the history hasn't been edited, so treat the list as
append only: you add to the end, and never change what's there.
Pause the video and predict.
A question needs three separate calculations, and the model asks for one per turn.
How many requests will the loop make?
And how many messages will the list hold at the end?
Four requests: three tool turns, plus one for the answer.
And eight messages: the question, then three pairs of request and result, then the
answer.
Quick check.
How does the loop know the agent has finished?
The reply contains no tool requests.
The model chose to answer instead, and the stop reason is end turn.
The loop decides, acts, observes, and repeats, always with a limit.
No tool requests means the model has answered.
Results go back as user messages, matched by ID.
And the history is append only.
Next lesson: everything that can go wrong in a loop, and how to stop safely.
